summary: Defines a Telnet option that enables a binary data mode between the two Telnet modules. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally Telnet sends typed letters. This option lets it send raw data of any kind.

questions: how to send binary data over telnet
what does iac iac mean in telnet
subtitle: The Telnet option that lets two ends agree to send raw 8-bit data instead of NVT ASCII text.

tldr.problem: Telnet normally carries text, but it is sometimes useful to have a binary path within Telnet without moving to a higher-level protocol such as FTP.
tldr.mechanism: The TRANSMIT-BINARY option, code 0, lets the two parties negotiate with WILL, WON'T, DO and DON'T to interpret received characters as 8 bits of binary data, separately for each direction.
tldr.outcome: In binary mode, IAC followed by IAC stands for the data value 255, and a later WON'T or DON'T reverts the encoding to NVT ASCII. It is an Internet Standard.

today: RFC 856 is an Internet Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Binary Transmission
sections.content:
The memo gives the option the name TRANSMIT-BINARY and the code 0. It is sometimes useful to have a binary path within TELNET without using a higher-level protocol such as the File Transfer Protocol.

The IAC prefix already used by TELNET makes this natural. Only a mechanism for the parties to agree to interpret the transmitted characters as binary data is needed. The memo specifies a standard for the ARPA Internet community, and hosts are expected to adopt and implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you want to send things that are not just letters. This option gives Telnet a way to do that without using another program.

sections.title: The Four Commands
sections.content:
IAC WILL TRANSMIT-BINARY requests permission to start, or confirms, sending characters that the receiver reads as 8 bits of binary data. IAC DO TRANSMIT-BINARY asks the other party to start sending binary data, or confirms it is expected to.

IAC WON'T and IAC DON'T mean different things depending on the current mode. If binary mode is already in operation, they demand a return to standard NVT ASCII. If not, they refuse or demand continuing in the present mode. A connection is in binary mode only when one party has requested it and the other has acknowledged it. The default is WON'T and DON'T, which means not binary.
sections.plainLanguage: One side asks, can we switch to raw data, and the other says yes or no. Either side can say stop, and then they go back to plain letters.

sections.title: How Data Is Interpreted
sections.content:
With the option in effect, the receiver should interpret characters not preceded by IAC as 8-bit binary data. The exception is IAC IAC, which stands for the 8-bit data value with decimal value 255.

An IAC followed by a real TELNET command is still a command in binary mode. An IAC followed by an undefined command has the same meaning as IAC NOP, though it should not normally be sent in this mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is treated as plain data, except a special signal byte. To send that byte as data, you send it twice.

sections.title: Implementation Suggestions
sections.content:
Implementations will probably refuse some other options, such as EBCDIC transmission, while binary mode is on, but a pair of hosts may negotiate combinations such as binary with echo. Binary mode must be negotiated separately for each direction of data flow, and the loop-preventing rules of the TELNET Protocol Specification apply.

The rule for WON'T and DON'T avoids a stack of past encodings. When not in binary mode, they mean continue in the current mode, whether NVT ASCII, EBCDIC or another. Once binary mode is agreed, a WON'T or DON'T reverts to NVT ASCII. Implementers should also consider whether terminals and processes can really pass all eight-bit characters. TOPS-20 is given as an example that intercepts some characters, such as ETX, and converts certain non-printing ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Both directions need their own agreement, and the computer in the middle must not secretly change your data. Stopping always goes back to plain letters.

viz.caption: THE FOUR TRANSMIT-BINARY COMMANDS (SUMMARISED FROM RFC 856)

cells: Sender requests or confirms that it will send 8-bit binary data
In binary mode, demands NVT ASCII; otherwise refuses to start binary
Sender requests or confirms that the data sender transmits binary
In binary mode, demands NVT ASCII; otherwise demands the present mode continue
